common_prompt:
Use case: stylized-concept. Asset type: one polished landscape environment concept painting for the Godot game Sparks & Machines, one full-bleed image, landscape 1536 by 1024, no collage. Input images are STYLE AND CONTINUITY REFERENCES ONLY, not an edit target: image 1 is the approved exterior of Nell's workshop on Spindle Lane; image 2 shows its adjoining houses. Invent a NEW city square as the very next block downhill from that exact neighbourhood. Keep the references' fine warm sepia outlines, softly bevelled chunky architectural forms, painterly plaster/stone/oak surfaces, individually laid terracotta roof tiles, teal shutters, cream and salmon and ochre facades, restrained brass fittings, warm summer daylight, cool soft shadows, hanging enamel signs, flowers and grounded everyday detail. Present it from the game's elevated three-quarter orthographic-like camera, high enough to understand doors, short connecting stairs, streets and walkable space. Aim for a richly finished playable environment concept, not a realistic photograph or a flat schematic.
CRITICAL REVISION: this is the active civic and trading centre of a MEDIUM-SIZED CITY, not a village green. Large, substantial THREE- TO FIVE-STOREY buildings share party walls and sit CLOSE TOGETHER. Rich shopfronts and inhabited upper floors, varied connected rooflines, dormers, chimneys, deep windows and balconies. The square is an enclosed, irregular urban room surrounded by a continuing town, with narrow streets visible between buildings. Avoid a row of isolated two-storey cottages, wide lawns, empty paving, a detached floating diorama or a remote harbour resort. Keep reference-scale doors and people: buildings grow by adding real floors and width, not by making humans child-sized.
A much LARGER, unmistakably eye-catching municipal POWER SOURCE anchors the middle: living roots carrying a warm amber spark, visibly enclosed in practical glass, stone, cream/teal enamel and restrained aged copper/brass infrastructure. It is an engineered, cared-for civic landmark with a coherent useful construction: an oversized readable dial, branch valves or service points, and inset brass conduits leaving through the paving. Give it a bold silhouette and a luminous amber heart visible in daylight. It should be large enough to be the city's meeting point and immediately command attention, while paths around it remain clear. No crystal obelisk, giant oak crown, swirling airborne magic, exposed dangerous reactor, neon or decorative gears everywhere.
The town must support later quests and money through its actual buildings: a civic quest-giving hall with a generous public entrance and notice/ticket counter; merchants' exchange or savings office; post/parcel service; bakery, grocer or bookshop, and occupied market stalls where transactions can happen. Distinct readable icons and varied entrances, without lots of written labels. Lived-in detail should equal or exceed the references: stocked stalls, realistic scales and crates, handcarts, bicycle, drain grilles, flowers on sills, worn doorsteps, washing between upper windows, supported wires, smoke, a few residents and cute small cream-and-teal worker automatons with WHEEL BASES. A tiny red-haired traveller in teal from the reference and Hotaru can supply scale, secondary to the architecture.
GEOGRAPHIC CONTINUITY MUST BE DRAWN: show the recognisable half-timbered cream workshop with terracotta roof, green double doors and round gable window on an adjoining UPPER COBBLED LANE, connected to this square by one short flight/turn of steps or a short descending street entirely visible in the SAME composition. It is one continuous tightly built hillside district, a one-minute walk, not a distant workshop on the horizon, a long monumental stair journey or an inset. Harbour only as a small background glimpse beyond rooftops. The tram's separate route need not enter this square.
All architecture must make physical sense, with supported balconies and awnings, real openings in walls, sagging supported laundry and wires, plausible pedestrian access and coherent steps. Clear silhouette hierarchy: power source first, major quest/civic building second, merchant frontage third. No game HUD, code editor, UI panels, map labels, numbered markers, watermarks or title text. Keep buildings fully legible rather than hiding the main district behind a huge foreground roof.

concepts.name: Founders' Court
concepts.design: An intimate horseshoe-shaped CIVIC COURT, enclosed on three sides by substantial joined four-storey plaster/timber townhouses. The major civic hall occupies a broad rear corner with a blue-slate roof, a modest clock turret, stone arch entrance and a covered public counter; the merchants' exchange and stocked corner shops fill the remaining frontages. In the middle stands THE GREAT GLASS ROOTWELL: a substantial stepped circular limestone plinth about six metres across, supporting a five-metre-high elongated bell of curved glass, divided by a few elegant dark-teal/copper ribs. A thick living root visibly curls around a LARGE molten-honey amber heart inside, with a heavy brass collar, low pressure dial and four useful branch valves. It is several people high and the clear focal point, not a little garden ornament. Market sellers hug the edges, leaving a lively walkable circuit around it. Nell's workshop is physically adjacent on the upper-left lane, its doors and familiar facade visible, with a single short dogleg stair running down along the side of the civic hall and opening directly into the court. Warm, welcoming, slightly irregular old city fabric with excellent silhouette clarity. This option should feel like the natural civic centre immediately below the approved workshop neighbourhood.

concepts.name: Market Cross
concepts.design: An energetic TRIANGULAR TRADING SQUARE where three narrow descending streets meet, enclosed by tall and slightly irregular attached four- and five-storey ochre, salmon and cream merchant houses, projecting bays, dormers and first-floor galleries. Give it a strong market identity: a large covered merchants' arcade along one edge, exchange/savings counter with an understated coin symbol, postal office, varied stocked stalls and an angled civic guild corner with a public ticket board and broad entrance. The central power landmark is THE ROOTWORKS LANTERN: an impressive six-metre-tall hexagonal glass lantern on a broad worked-stone base, with a strong green-copper crown, tall warm amber core cradled by living roots, a few structural ribs, a monumental cream pressure dial at eye level and visibly connected branch lines in the ground. A landmark with the presence of a small civic tower, not a little fountain. Stalls and café tables cluster at the perimeter, people can circle the lantern. The triangular geometry and diagonal urban lanes distinguish this option from a symmetrical court. Nell's exact workshop is drawn at the top of a short cobbled slope entering from the left, only the adjoining block away; the whole short route is visible between continuous connected buildings. Keep an inhabited mid-century harbour city, detailed and bright, without picturesque empty space or rural lawns.

concepts.name: Terraced Exchange
concepts.design: A rich TWO-LEVEL URBAN SQUARE built into the hill rather than set apart from it. An upper civic terrace fronts a substantial four-storey town hall and postal offices; a lower market court fronts a long three-storey arcaded merchants' exchange with occupied counters and taller attached townhouses behind. One generous broad stair and a shorter side stair connect the levels visibly. Make the power source THE ROOTWORKS ROTUNDA, a spectacular two-storey-height stone-and-copper civic conservatory about eight metres across, straddling the level change: large clear curved glass panels reveal a tangled living root spiralling around a brilliant amber heart, beneath a patinated copper cupola. Its lower stone drum exposes broad gauges and service windows facing the market; the upper gallery provides an accessible balcony around its glass, reached from the upper square. It is one coherent impressive municipal machine/pavilion, not a collection of decorative gears or two unrelated fountains. Brass supply branches follow the stair sides and descend beneath the market paving. Dense three-to-five-storey facades enclose both levels, with built-in shops, archways and excellent lived-in work details. The upper terrace directly CONTINUES Spindle Lane: draw Nell's recognizable workshop and adjoining stone house at the near end of that upper street, seamlessly adjoining the civic buildings. The player can visibly walk from the shop along the terrace and down into the square in a handful of turns. Preserve the approved area's style and human scale. This alternative should feel like the most natural use of a hillside, with the landmark linking the two levels.

concepts.name: Lantern Exchange
concepts.design: A compact ROUNDED CITY PLAZA, with a continuous curved frontage of substantial four- and five-storey merchant and civic buildings, narrow alleys cutting between them, and an elegant public arcade wrapping one side. Stronger urban density than the other options, still warm and human rather than grand imperial stone. Give the public exchange hall a generous covered entrance and street-facing money counter under an understated coin emblem; post office, bakery and civic quest office have distinct doors and signs. The centre is THE FOUNDERS' BEACON, a landmark around nine metres high: a wide octagonal limestone service base, cream enamel and green-copper structural pillars supporting an immense rounded amber GLASS LANTERN CHAMBER, a living root rising visibly through its core, a domed copper cap and a few connecting braces. It is an everyday city's power landmark, beautifully maintained, with an enormous readable gauge on its base and working access, without military or industrial menace. Four clear conduits emerge into the cobbles and everyday benches and notice stands gather around its foot. The landmark should establish a strong vertical silhouette against the surrounding roofline while its upper glass still stays below the tallest nearby buildings. Nell's approved half-timbered workshop is just up a SHORT rising street at the back-left opening of the curved frontage, clearly visible together with its stone neighbour and one turn of stairs: their doors and pavement are part of the same connected block, not a remote skyline element. Leave the walking circuit readable, with bustling trade at the edges, dense windows, awnings, upper-floor laundry, bicycles and small rolling service robots. This is the most city-centre and instantly recognizable meeting-point direction.
